But paradise has been lost, and its loss brings about the phenomenon of death. This is why Milton so firmly maintains the idea of the complete resurrection of the whole human being, following the complete death of that human being. He holds, of course, that time—as the measure of movement, marked by the revolutions of the stars—does not exist for the dead. Consequently, those who are resurrected will awaken as though they had only just died. It is here, it seems to me, that Qâzî Sa'îd’s doctrine of the time of the Malakût can help bring this Image of the whole human being into clearer focus. For Qâzî Sa'îd would agree with the anthropology professed by Milton.

The complete human being consists of a triad: spirit, soul, and body. This triad already exists here and now, each of its elements possessing its own allotted measure, in conformity with the conditions required by our sensible material world, the molk. Resurrection is the passage of this entire triad from its present condition in the sensible material world into the state of the Malakût. It is, by that very fact, the definitive passage from the “opaque and dense” time of our world into the subtle time of the Malakût. And death is nothing other than this passage.

The reader of Qâzî Sa'îd may therefore wonder whether Milton stops too soon. Why should resurrection still be regarded as something to be awaited after death? Why should we suppose that there is an interval separating us from it, an interval measurable in the units of our “opaque and dense” time, with the simple qualification “as though” attempting to abolish that interval? Such a conception would be understandable if resurrection took place on this side of Mount Qâf. But resurrection takes place beyond Mount Qâf. On the graves of those who lived before our post-Christian age, one can often read an inscription such as:

The reader of Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî will have the impression that the roles have been reversed. Those who are waiting are the ones who still inhabit “opaque and dense” time, those whose time has not yet folded back into the time of the Malakût.

But for those who have departed, the event has already taken place. They are within the time of the Malakût, which is no longer a time of waiting. We have seen that Solomon has already been resurrected in the Malakût. The end of “opaque and dense” time does not come about through an accumulation of centuries upon centuries. Such time would remain exactly what it was even if we moved to another planet. Its end lies in the “involution of time”—in the passage into the Malakût and into the time of the Malakût. This is the meaning of the Prophet’s saying: Man mâta faqad qâmat qiyâmatuh. Whoever has died has already entered upon his resurrection. The correspondence I have just tried to sketch is only one example. Almost everything along this path remains to be done.

But perhaps this example will be enough to suggest that, when certain theologians of our day—usually hostile to anything reminiscent of Platonism—systematically oppose the immortality of the soul to the resurrection of the dead, the materials on which they base their conclusions are far from complete.

By contrast, the magnificent hymn to Light at the beginning of Book III of Paradise Lost vibrates with an esoteric presentiment of the Malakût, written by a poet whose eyes could no longer see the light of this world:

So much the rather thou Celestial Light Shine inward, and the mind through all her powers Irradiate, there plant eyes, all mist from thence Purge and disperse, that I may see and tell Of things invisible to mortal sight.

If the preceding pages have brought certain essential features of Shiite thought and spirituality into focus, it should not be difficult to see where the Shaykhi school belongs within them, why it matters, and why this book could not leave it out. We should not pretend, however, that the work is nearly finished. Much research remains to be done before we can understand the school in detail and trace its roots in the spiritual knowledge—the gnosis—taught by the holy Imams.

The terms Shaykhism and Shaykhi school follow common usage in Iran, Iraq, and India. The school came to be known by these names because of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î, regarded as the shaykh above all others and therefore as its founder.

Yet he never set out to “found” a new and separate school. His sole purpose was to remain completely faithful to the spiritual and philosophical teaching of the holy Imams of Twelver Shiism, and to bring that teaching back to life in its fullness. It might therefore be more accurate to speak of integralism, provided we understand the word in its original sense—preserving something whole—and do not burden it with the emotional and political associations it has acquired in the modern West. Shaykhi integralism was not concerned with upholding doctrines laid down by a Church, rescuing a threatened liturgy, or defending a crumbling religious hierarchy.

What it opposed, above all, was a pious agnosticism content with the outward forms and rules of religion, and a theological rationalism that had closed itself off from the deeper sources of inner life. Its defining commitment was an unconditional respect for the entire spiritual tradition inherited from the Imams, together with the form of spiritual life inseparable from that tradition. Taken together, these make possible an Imami Shiism preserved in its full and undiminished form: the “perfect Shiism” whose technical meaning merely confirms the original sense of shi'a, the “followers of the holy Imams.”

The contrast becomes clearer when we consider the transformation Twelver Shiism underwent under the Safavids. Having always been a minority religion, it became the state religion of Iran in the opening years of the sixteenth century. We have already touched on this transformation elsewhere in this work.

Some form of official “clergy” was bound to emerge, even though there was no Church in the Christian sense. And with an official clergy came an “orthodoxy” of the kind that, wherever it arises, tends to distrust gnosis, theosophy, and the mysticism of individual salvation. When people look only at this outward aspect of the change, they too often content themselves with a sociological or political explanation.

But that is to see religion only from the outside. It misses what religious consciousness itself is directed toward and, with it, what makes Shiite religious life distinctive. Such explanations do at least bring something important into view: the very outward structure against which Shiism, understood as a religious idea, is inevitably engaged in struggle.

The preceding discussion should have guarded us against some widespread misunderstandings of what lies at the heart of Shiism. The issue is not a political dispute within the history of our world. It is not simply the “legitimacy” of the descendants of Ali, nor merely how much reverence is due to the Ahl al-Bayt, the members of the Prophet's household. Something quite different is at stake.

We can begin to sense it when we recognize that the governing theme of the entire teaching is Imamology—the understanding of the Imams and their spiritual significance—and that this theme sounds through every “octave” of the universe. Since the prophetic message of the final Prophet, twelve Imams have fulfilled the initiatory role of spiritual guides.

The last is the Imam of our time, the Hidden Imam, who dwells in the mystical world of Hûrqâlyâ. Together with the Prophet himself and Fâtima the Radiant (al-Zahrâ)—his daughter and the source of the Imams' line, called the “meeting place of the two Lights,” the light of prophecy and the light of spiritual initiation (majma' al-nûrayn)—they form the fullness, or pleroma, of the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones.”
Yet we do not understand this sacred company primarily by considering the brief earthly lives of its members.

We must contemplate what these persons are as eternal beings, existing before the cosmos. Their level of being is the Lâhût, the divine sphere, which stands above the Jabarût, the realm of the pure angelic Intelligences. Beneath that lies the Malakût, the world of the Soul and of imaginative perception; beneath it, the Molk, the sensible world brought forth through the activity of the Soul.

At the level of the Lâhût, the Fourteen Immaculate Ones are the primordial manifestation of God—the first theophany—in the Haqîqat mohammadîya, the eternal Muhammadan Reality. They are the divine Names and Attributes, the only aspects of the divine that our knowledge and devotion can reach. As the instruments through which the divine becomes manifest, they are also the only conceivable means by which the divine can enter into relation with human beings in this earthly world. Through their activity, the cosmos itself comes into being.

When contemplated in this way, in their eternal essence and personhood, the Fourteen Immaculate Ones occupy a level of existence comparable, in a certain sense, to the Aeons of Valentinian Gnosticism. If Imamology has a role in Shiite theology corresponding to that of Christology in Christian theology, the closer comparison is with a Gnostic form of Christology—or, better still, with a wisdom centered on the figure of Christ, a Christosophy. All these universes are related to one another through symbols. Each has its own heavens and earth, arranged in an order that reproduces the succession of the primordial divine manifestations.

The pattern governing the supreme pleroma of the Lâhût is thus repeated as we descend from world to world, until at last it unfolds in the dimension of earthly time. (See, in the preceding book, pp. 185 ff., the “Twelve Veils of Light”: the twelve Imamic universes through which the Muhammadan Light passes before appearing in this world.) The essential task of esoteric interpretation, or ta'wîl, is to discover within historical time a pattern of succession that corresponds to the structure of the pleroma. It is to uncover the true, hidden meaning: the enduring spiritual history, the parable that shines through the account of outward, material events. This is something altogether different from tracing “historical currents” or “influences” along a single chain of cause and effect confined to the sensible, material world.

We are dealing instead with a history that has several dimensions, including the dimension beyond ordinary history—metahistory. To move between these dimensions, we must perceive an underlying structure that remains constant, an isomorphism. Think of a melody played at different pitches: the individual notes change, but their relationships remain the same. It is still the same melody, the same musical figure, the same form.

Yet if we are to understand Imamology on this scale, extending through every universe, we must accept the whole body of traditions handed down under the names of the holy Imams, as the Shaykhi school does. Once criticism of these traditions gives way to unacknowledged rationalist assumptions, this entire theosophical vision of the Imams disappears. With it disappears the understanding of the spiritual or esoteric meaning (bâtin) of the Quranic revelation and of the earlier prophetic revelations—and therefore the practice of ta'wîl, their spiritual interpretation.

Shiite thinkers had, of course, accomplished an immense amount in the roughly three centuries between Nasîroddîn Tûsî and the Safavid restoration. We should recall here 'Allâmeh Hillî, Rajab Borsî, Haydar Âmolî, Sâ'inoddîn Ispahânî, Ibn Abî Jomhûr, and many others. Their work bore fruit in the philosophical schools that subsequently flourished, above all in the thought of Mîr Dâmâd and the School of Isfahan, which we have already discussed. This philosophical renaissance remains a distinctive feature of Iranian Islam, without parallel elsewhere in the Islamic world.

But the Safavid restoration brought two developments at once. It created favorable conditions for Shiite philosophy, or philosophical Shiism, while also confronting it—at the very moment when it was emerging, so to speak, from concealment—with the organization of the Safavid state's official Shiism. Inevitably, Mullâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, his students, and their successors encountered considerable difficulties with the official “clergy.”

To some extent they too had to practice taqîyeh: the discipline of concealing inward beliefs and teachings. For official Shiism had then undergone a development all too familiar elsewhere in Islam: the growing dominance of fiqh, religious law and jurisprudence, until these threatened to become synonymous with theology itself. Understanding does not come easily between the foqahâ, scholars concerned exclusively with religious law, and the 'orafâ, mystics devoted to spiritual knowledge and theosophy.

Yet from generation to generation, right down to our own day, the effort of the 'orafâ and the followers of hikmat ilâhîya has never ceased. As we have had occasion to emphasize, hikmat ilâhîya is not quite what we mean by either philosophy or theology. It is a search for divine wisdom that embraces and transcends both—literally, a theosophia, for which the Arabic expression is an exact equivalent of the Greek.

Unfortunately, because the official religious establishment was absorbed in legal learning and the formal distinctions of case-based jurisprudence, anyone who pursued this wisdom risked being suspected of undermining religious belief by introducing philosophy. Mullâ Sadrâ had already denounced this confusion in impassioned passages echoing what Haydar Âmolî had written some three centuries earlier. To abandon everything that belonged to 'irfân, inner spiritual knowledge, would have been to mutilate the most precious part of the Imams' inheritance.

How could those who knew so many sayings of the Imams—the very sources of “Imamic theosophy”—possibly consent to that? In a sense, Shiism was compelled to conceal part of itself even from itself, and to preserve its character as an esoteric religion. Its followers found themselves in the position that seekers of gnosis have faced everywhere and in every age.

This brief sketch of the situation—a familiar subject of conversation in Iran—also helps us locate the Shaykhi school. Above all, its determination to restore Imamism in its entirety makes it a metaphysical and spiritual re-formation, something of a very different order from the modern “reformist” movements found elsewhere in Islam, many of which emerged under Western influence.

The Shaykhis sought a spiritual philosophy drawn exclusively from the words of the Imams and rejected the predominance of legal questions and considerations. Most mojtaheds, the jurists empowered to exercise independent legal judgment, could hardly be expected to understand that intention at once. More precisely, the Shaykhis were raising questions the jurists' habits of mind left them unable to accommodate—questions all the more alarming because they called the jurists' own role into question.

This does not mean, however, that Shaykhism simply joined the camp of the philosophers and spiritual thinkers associated with Mullâ Sadrâ's school, whether Avicennian or ishrâqî (followers of the philosophy of Illumination). There are certainly points of intersection, but for the Shaykhis the sources remain the texts of the holy Imams alone; their method of thought is far more interpretive—hermeneutical, in the Stoic manner—than dialectical. An equal distance separates Shaykhism from Sufism.

The place given to a shaykh within Sufi tarîqat, or spiritual orders, seems to the Shaykhis to usurp the authority of the Hidden Imam: it makes the Sufi master a substitute for the Imam, which is incompatible with the meaning of his ghaybat, his occultation or concealment. Rather, the devout Shiite and the Shiite seeker can have only one shaykh: the Imam himself, their personal guide, the “invisible master who is present in the heart.”

The result is a distinctive kind of doctrine and spiritual life. It shares certain features with the philosophers—notably the ishrâqîyûn, the Illuminationists—and with the Sufis, yet it takes the form of neither, because it is shaped entirely by the teaching of the Imams. We have already noted that Sufism (tasawwof) does not encompass every form of mystical life in Islam.

And here the difficulties of research begin. The teaching of the Imams forms an enormous body of writings. It includes not only the texts preserved in Majlisî's great encyclopedia, but also those scattered through other collections, especially traditional reports (hadith, or akhbâr) in which the “Gnostic” tendencies are particularly evident. These latter texts call for extensive investigation, beginning with the ways Ismaili writers made use of them. This body of writings is more than the foundation for interpreting the Quran's hidden meaning in accordance with the teaching of the Imams; it amounts to an entire encyclopedia of knowledge. It is to this body of texts that Shaykhi scholars refer whenever they declare their fidelity to the Imams' teaching in its entirety.
We shall have occasion later to explain why and how the Shaykhi position toward these writings overcomes the opposition between the akhbârî and osûlî schools.
The first question a historian of religions is likely to ask concerns how this body of writings was formed.

But even if we could reconstruct perfectly every stage through which these traditional reports were transmitted and compiled, we would still have approached them only from the outside. To understand what role they play in the religious consciousness of Shiism, we would need instead to uncover the overall structure of the collection: how its different themes are grouped, how they recur, what concerns give them their shape, and so on. Shiite authors themselves offer some clues.

Khwânsârî, for example, provides several, while showing a respect and admiration for the person and writings of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î that stand in marked contrast to the hostility through which others have misled unwary researchers. His indications show that, although the Shaykhi school aims at restoration and renewal, it does not represent a doctrinal innovation within Imamism. It rightly claims the whole tradition of Shiite theosophy, reaching back to its earliest witnesses.

So many eminent names appear even in the incomplete list Khwânsârî gives from memory that it would be rash to condemn Shaykhism as gholow, or “extremism.” As we have already said, what is at issue is not “extremism” but “integralism,” in the word's original sense. The term describes both a fact and the intention behind it: the desire to preserve an entire tradition. That desire gives no grounds for passing a disparaging judgment on a school that remains an integral part of Shiism.

Unfortunately, judgments of this kind seem to have led astray the few Orientalists who have so far paid any attention to Shaykhism, preventing them from sensing the profound spiritual worth that deserves their sympathy. For our part, we confess that we have never really understood the passions this school has aroused.

Considerations appear to have entered the debate that have little to do with the life of the spirit—the only concern proper to a philosopher and a scholar of religion. We have also had to acknowledge that the kinds of attacks directed at Shaykhi doctrines give us no reason to believe their authors had read the books closely, or truly understood what they were attacking. Some judgments are so strange that one wonders whether they were made under the necessity of ketmân, or taqîyeh: the discipline of esoteric concealment prescribed by the Imams and made especially necessary by the circumstances described above.

We hear, for instance, that Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î was certainly a very holy man, but no metaphysical philosopher. Even the short extract from one of his books that we shall present below would be enough to disprove that. We hear that he understood neither the problems nor the technical language of the philosophers—of Mullâ Sadrâ, for example, on two of whose works he wrote substantial critical commentaries.

Yet Shaykh Ahmad himself discussed those questions and that vocabulary with complete command, and showed a clear understanding of how his own terminology and way of posing the problems differed from theirs. We even hear that, although the shaykh was undoubtedly wholly faithful to the teaching of the Imams, he did not really understand their texts either. We still await even the beginnings of evidence for that charge.

In any case, the Imams' words can be interpreted on several levels of understanding. It is arbitrary to treat fidelity to a tradition and originality of thought as incompatible. To reproach a thinker for his originality is to reproach him for following his vocation—and, in the end, to mistake a living tradition for a funeral procession.

There is no need to linger over these distressing controversies. We have mentioned them because they have made it harder for researchers to gain access to the Shaykhi school's authentic thought. The texts themselves are difficult, and its books are hardly to be found on ordinary bookshop shelves. Its questions and its whole technical vocabulary must be learned before they can be understood. So it is not altogether surprising that serious study has scarcely begun. Bábism and the Bahá'í faith, on the other hand, have received attention, notably from E. G. Browne. Often, by repeating or intensifying hasty and passionate judgments, writers have held Shaykhism “responsible” for them.

We shall have occasion to explain again why, however interesting these religious movements may be in their own right, they cannot possibly be regarded as “offspring” of the Shaykhi school. If this claim is the principal reason for the accusations against Shaykhism, critics should at least begin by taking seriously the books in which the Shaykhis have set out to show—and to prove—that these alleged offspring are not theirs. Scholarly fairness demands as much.

The shaykhs who led this school left behind a vast body of work: some thousand writings, of which only about a third have been published, the rest surviving in manuscript. The first three shaykhs were naturally of foremost importance: Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1753–1826), his first successor Sayyed Kâzem Reshtî (1798–1843), and then Shaykh Mohammad Karîm-Khân Kermânî (1809–1870), who belonged by birth to the Qajar imperial family. They and their successors were as remarkable for nobility and strength of character as for their astonishing literary productivity.

The autobiographical material we possess from the first three shaykhs helps us understand the deep reaches of consciousness beyond ordinary awareness from which Shiite devotion to the holy Imams arises. That devotion already finds expression in the visionary pattern of their adolescent dreams; it cannot be separated from the lofty spiritual philosophy we have just recalled in outline.

Part of the account that follows grew out of the publication, some fifteen years ago, of a substantial Persian work by the then leader of the Shaykhi community, Shaykh Sarkâr Âghâ, who died recently, in December 1969. He undertook it in response to a request from those responsible for the library of the shrine of Imam Rezâ in Mashhad, who were then preparing its catalogues. The work offers both an excellent account of the present state of scholarship and an indispensable introduction to Shaykhism—and therefore to the study of Shiism over the last two centuries.

For the first time, it brings together, in sequence, biographies of the great mashâyekh, the leading shaykhs who have ensured the school's continuity down to our own day, alongside a systematic and comprehensive bibliography of their works in Persian and Arabic, whether published or still unpublished. We would therefore like to outline these biographies, enriched by previously unpublished documents, and give some indication of the monumental writings each shaykh left behind.

At the end we shall be able to dwell on only a few points of doctrine; these will serve as the sketch of a program for future research. Naturally, we cannot attempt here a systematic comparison with the more or less reliable accounts of historians who do not belong to the Shaykhi school. Our purpose is to present the school's own perspective, the understanding of itself expressed in Shaykh Sarkâr Âghâ's work.
2. The Life and Work of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î

The biographical section of this great work follows a plan that reveals a distinctive sense of history and of time, worthy of a phenomenological study in its own right. It begins in the present and works backward, shaykh by shaykh, to the founder—the reverse of the approach familiar to historians who normally begin with origins. Here we think it better to set aside that movement backward through time and follow a chronological order more in keeping with our usual habits.

Although most biographical collections include an entry on Shaykh Ahmad, they must be used with care and discrimination. As Sarkâr Âghâ observes (pp. 164 ff.), their authors most often know nothing of the terms and problems of hikmat, spiritual philosophy, and even less, if possible, of Shaykh Ahmad's own distinctive language. The misunderstandings are compounded by inadequate information and superficial observation.

Certain propositions, for example, originated in Sunni thought but gradually came to be taken for granted without Shiites even realizing their source. Shaykh Ahmad's departure from such propositions therefore need not have the significance that an ill-informed writer might assign to it. Fortunately, we have first-hand information of unquestionable authenticity. There is Shaykh Ahmad's autobiography, recovered by Sarkâr Âghâ, which gives a detailed account of the mystical experiences of his youth and already traces the entire course his life would take.

In addition, three contemporary treatises provide a body of information corroborated by testimony passed down through the generations within the Shaykhi community. And there is one further indispensable source for his biography: Shaykh Ahmad's own writings. Many of his treatises were composed in response to questions put to him by contemporaries. We should study these exchanges closely, both to see how he clarified his teaching and to understand the response it drew from those around him.

Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î was born in 1166 AH (1753) in a small settlement near al-Ahsâ', in the territory of Bahrain. He traced his ancestry back ten generations, to the second half of the fifteenth century, and came from an entirely Arab family.

But this was eastern Arabia, along the Persian Gulf, a region where historians have seldom thought to look for philosophers and thinkers. The name al-Ahsâ', however, is not without symbolic resonance in the history of Islamic gnosis. In the eleventh century, Nâsir-e Khosraw gave a lengthy account in his travel journal of the remarkably ideal conditions he found in the small Qarmatian state he visited and admired. Nor should we forget that it was during the roughly fifteen years Shaykh Ahmad spent in Iran that his teaching inspired the response and enthusiasm without which there would probably never have been a movement called “Shaykhism.”

Moreover, since the time of his second successor, the Shaykhi school's center has been in Kerman, in southeastern Iran, where it has a theological school, a college, and a printing press. We should also bear in mind that, at the time of writing, Iran officially maintains special ties with Bahrain, recalling the period when Bahrain formed part of its territory.

More important for understanding Shaykh Ahmad's character, however, are the considerations suggested by his autobiography, rediscovered in his own handwriting. Sarkâr Âghâ originally intended to publish it in Persian translation, but happily decided instead to reproduce the Arabic original (pp. 166–179). Shaykh Ahmad wrote it at the request of one of his sons, Shaykh Mohammad Taqî. It records many traits that, as in the lives of spiritual figures from other cultures, reveal an aptitude for mystical experience from childhood onward.

While playing with boys of his own age, young Ahmad would often suddenly leave them. Some familiar object had appeared to him in a strange new light; that alone was enough to draw him away into solitude and keep him there in prolonged meditation. He especially loved to dream among the traces of abandoned encampments, among the ruins of temporary dwellings built from perishable materials. His imagination would lose itself in melancholy recollections, accompanied by abundant tears.

The fire of a secret passion consumed him. Those around him showed little concern for religious thought or observance. Young and old, however, liked to gather frequently for noisy entertainments filled with singing and instrumental music. Ahmad could not keep himself from joining in, only to find, when alone again, that he was torn between a resolution never to go back and a secret desire to return. Then something apparently trivial happened. One day a man whose name he does not give asked him to help compose a poem.

But Ahmad knew nothing of grammar. Fortunately, a young companion was studying the subject with a local shaykh, one Shaykh Mohammad ibn Shaykh Mohsin. Ahmad borrowed a text from him—the 'Awâmil of Jorjânî—and copied it out in full. His parents later found him asleep with the pages gripped tightly in his hand. So it was decided that he too should go and study with the same shaykh.

He would never have admitted his desire to study, any more than he would have confessed to anyone his secret attraction to the gatherings that afterward filled him with such remorse. Many years had to pass before he could overcome his extreme reserve and bring himself to tell his son, in detail, of the visionary experiences of his adolescence. That account is an invaluable document for the psychology of religious experience.

Although his entire teaching can be described as an integral Imamology, it was not a theory constructed late in life from books. It was a lived experience, born with the awakening of his consciousness and rooted in the mystery of his personal calling. We might say that, from his youth, Shaykh Ahmad embodied the fundamental Imami religious feeling from which the doctrine itself springs. He gives brief accounts of some ten visions.

Together they reveal a consciousness mysteriously and completely possessed by the spiritual archetypes represented by the holy Imams. These visions were preceded by a number of prophetic dreams. The first was of a young man holding a book, who proceeded to give a remarkable ta'wîl, or spiritual interpretation, of two Quranic verses (87:2–3), drawing from them a profound philosophical teaching. After this, young Ahmad felt a thoroughgoing distaste for the study of grammar and philology pursued as ends in themselves.

He began visiting various shaykhs, but not one could teach him anything resembling what he had heard in his dream. As a result, he withdrew further and further from those around him. He was present among his family only “in body.” “At that time I saw so many things that I cannot possibly tell of them all.” Among “these things,” one image recurred: he would climb onto the roof terrace of a house or ascend the summit of a high mountain.

A mysterious object would descend from the sky, something intangible and unreal, and he would have to grasp it. Then one night he entered a mosque “in a vision.” There he found himself before three figures, whom he learned to be the Second Imam, Hasan ibn 'Alî; the Fourth, 'Alî ibn Hosayn Zayn al-'Âbidîn; and the Fifth, Mohammad Bâqir. This vision marked the beginning of a whole series of dreams in which he received personal spiritual initiation.

The first such “meeting” recalls certain features of Mîr Dâmâd's vision in the mosque at Qomm (see above, Book V, Chapter 1, section 2). Ahmad asked Imam Hasan to teach him a prayer in the form of a poem that he could recite whenever he wished the Imam to appear. He was taught the words and has preserved the complete text for us.

Yet however faithfully he recited them, the vision did not return. At last he understood what the Imam had intended: that Ahmad should bring his entire inner being into harmony with the spiritual meaning hidden in the poem.

As he was to explain years later in a letter to a friend, a letter confirming his autobiography point by point, it was this inward condition, this fundamental “perfect harmony,” that made the visions that followed possible. He wrote: “It is related that Imam Mohammad Bâqir said: If one of the faithful loves us, grows in love for us, and devotes himself to knowing us, there is no question he can ask without our inspiring its answer in his heart. Then things were opened to me that I do not know how to describe to other people.

“All of it arose because I had brought my inner being into harmony with the spiritual meaning of the poem Imam Hasan had taught me.” A life of intimacy now began with each of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones: the Prophet, Fâtima al-Zahrâ, and all twelve Imams, including the Hidden Imam. “I saw strange and marvelous dreams in the heavens, in the paradises, in the world beyond the senses and in the barzakh—the intermediate realm—figures and colors that dazzled the mind” (p. 175).
These dreams can rightly be called “initiatory.”

Indeed, the teaching Shaykh Ahmad later developed across so many books cannot be separated from the instruction he received in them. He himself wrote: “Whenever a problem held me back in waking life, I would see its explanation in a dream, whenever, having called the holy Imams to mind in my dream, I saw one of them” (p. 181). “Then the question appeared to me together with every proof supporting it, so that, even if the whole world had joined forces against me, no one could have made me doubt it, because I had seen” (p. 177).

The culmination of these visionary experiences came when Shaykh Ahmad dreamed of the Tenth Imam holding a bundle of papers: these were the ijâzât, the authorizations or licenses granted to him by each of the Twelve Imams (p. 178).

We can do no more than register this spiritual fact and ask not so much what explains it as what it implies. Every one of these dreams was an occasion of instruction that would later find its way into his writings. In his autobiography he told his son: “If you wish to understand that what I say is sincere, study carefully the books in which I discuss philosophy.

“In most of these books, and on most questions, my position differs from the solutions given by the philosophers and by the scholastic theologians (motakallimûn). Once you have thoroughly reflected on my teaching, you will see that it agrees with the traditions of our guiding Imams, and you will not find a single point where it contradicts them.

“On the other hand, you will discover that most philosophers and scholastic theologians contradict the teachings and traditions of the Imams. If you want to understand why, have the fairness to acknowledge the truth of what I am telling you, for I never speak without a proof drawn from the Imams.”

Shaykh Ahmad's experience, like that of all the great visionary mystics, has the character of an archetypal phenomenon, as impossible to reduce to something else as the perception of a sound or a color. A phenomenology of religious experience can only attend to descriptions of such experiences and to what they imply. It must not try to derive them from something else, or explain them away through imagined chains of cause and effect. Its task is to discover what form of consciousness makes possible the perception of events and worlds inaccessible to ordinary consciousness today.

Indeed, Shaykhi ontology and cosmology give special attention to the mode of existence of the “intermediate world,” which establishes and guarantees the validity of visionary perceptions. Throughout his life, Shaykh Ahmad maintained absolute confidence in the ijâzât granted to him by the holy Imams in that intermediate world.

In every branch of knowledge and every matter, he invoked the Imams as his support, his authority, and his source (istinâd and i'timâd), calling to mind what they had revealed to him in his visionary states. His entire consciousness rested upon his visions, which, he repeatedly testified, taught him things he had never heard from any shaykh. Visions, revelations, dreams: here they take the archetypal forms proper to Shiite consciousness. These are spiritual facts that cannot be treated lightly. As Sarkâr Âghâ reminds us, numerous traditional reports, or akhbâr, attest that “the visions of the perfected believer (mûmin kâmil) have the value of direct perception” (p. 185).

Yet Shaykh Ahmad was right to close the short spiritual autobiography written for his son with these words: “Such things are not well suited to explanation, especially to the ignorant and the envious” (p. 179).

In any case, apart from the rather obscure shaykh who taught him grammar as a boy, Shaykh Ahmad nowhere names a particular master whose acknowledged disciple he had been or from whom he had received his spiritual authorization. Nor does the Shaykhi community's own tradition identify any shaykh whose name he personally invoked as the source of his authority, his istinâd. This would later be the case for Sayyed Kâzem in relation to Shaykh Ahmad, for Shaykh Mohammad Karîm-Khân Kermânî in relation to Sayyed Kâzem, and for so many other spiritual seekers in relation to their masters.

At most, we find a passing reference that hints at a brief encounter with far-reaching consequences. Shaykh Ahmad may therefore be counted among those whom Iranians call the Owaysîs: people whose only true spiritual master has been the shaykh al-ghayb or ostâd-e ghaybî, the guide in the world beyond the senses, the inward and personal master. Shaykh Ahmad himself tells us who that unseen guide was in his case. In doing so, he reveals the deeper meaning of Shiism's method of spiritual guidance, as we recalled above, and the bond between speculative Imamology and inward experience.

This did not prevent him from being in contact with numerous teachers. He exchanged questions and answers with shaykhs and other eminent figures, who expressed their agreement with his views (tasdîqât) and their reverence for him. This was true of his early stays in Iraq as well as his long periods in Iran. Over the years distinguished shaykhs awarded him detailed ijâzât, authorizations whose texts would fill a whole volume if reproduced in full.

Accordingly, he referred to this entire body of authorizations, but never singled out one named master. That attitude accords perfectly with what Shaykhism would call the “Fourth Pillar” of Shiite doctrine: no individual teacher's authority can ever be “substituted” for the prerogative of the Imam (see Chapter III below). In any event, no one ever doubted his extraordinary learning or spiritual distinction.

His first contacts outside his homeland bear this out. He remained in Bahrain until about the age of twenty, leading a life that, although we lack detailed information about it, we may imagine to have been devoted chiefly to meditation. Did he set out because a compelling command received in a vision made him sense a calling to teach, despite his own preference for solitude? Whatever the reason, in 1186 AH (1772) Shaykh Ahmad departed for the Shiite holy places in Iraq.

Many celebrated scholars were gathered there at the time, and he entered into sustained discussions and scholarly meetings with them. Attending the majlis, or learned gathering, of Sayyed Mahdî Tabâtabâ'î, he asked him for an ijâzat and presented one of his own works, a commentary on 'Allâmeh Hillî's Tabsira. After reading it, the Sayyed told him: “O Shaykh! It is you who should be granting me an ijâzat” (p. 204).

To his own students he declared: “This shaykh is a Sign (âyat) among the Signs of God. It is extraordinary that he should have been born and raised in a country generally lacking in learning and philosophy, where people know only a few questions concerning ritual prayer.

“The appearance of a person so complete, uniting every kind of excellence, can be explained only as a divine grace.” He added: “I myself cannot understand this shaykh's loftier problems, for I know only fiqh and the osûl,” jurisprudence and its principles (ibid.). If only all jurists and specialists in fiqh had shown the same modesty before passing judgment on the shaykh's teachings!

For what delighted those around him was that God had raised up an Imami scholar who knew the spiritual wisdom handed down from the holy Imams and could debate on equal terms with the philosophers and the motakallimûn, the scholastic theologians. Instead of pronouncing curses and accusations of unbelief (takfîr), like so many mullahs concerned only with law, or even forbidding philosophy itself, he could meet these thinkers on their own ground.
